notes: Settings now move between browsers, which they never really did. Each shortcut opens a browser profile of its own and no profile can read another's storage, so the settings file beside index.html is the only thing all of them can see -- and Export was saving it into the Downloads folder, where nothing ever read it. That is why settings exported from Chrome never turned up in Edge. Each profile is now told to save into the app folder, and the file is read at every launch rather than once on a fresh profile: it is imported whenever its contents differ from the last version that browser took, so settings changed in one browser and not exported are left alone, and exporting is the deliberate act that says this file is now the word. Whoever exported last wins. An export also carries everything now. Whether the schedule was switched on was being written into the file and thrown away on the way back in, so a schedule exported running came back stopped, silently, with the drawer looking as though it had forgotten; the level and the tone travelled the same way. Every file is stamped with the version that wrote it and the date and time to the second, two files on a desktop can therefore be told apart, and importing says which version the file came from. Older exports are read and brought forward without asking. The next-up chip no longer calls a gap free play. A gap in the middle of the day is not the end of the day, so the setting that can turn the radio off does not apply to it and whatever is on keeps playing -- but the chip said "Free play", which is the name of the other setting word for word, and five minutes between two slots was enough to make the drawer look as though it were lying about being set to turn off. A gap now says so and says what it means for the sound; "Free play" is said only when the day has really ended and the setting really is Keep playing. The installer runs the published copy of itself. It ships inside the zip, so the copy in an app folder is always one release behind the thing it is about to install, and a fix to the way installing works could never reach the run that needed it. It now fetches the newest one, compares it byte for byte, and hands the job over if they differ -- one request, before anything is written, from the same release as the zip full of code it was going to unpack anyway. It says which version it is putting in and which one that replaces, read out of the archive already on the disk. With no shortcut on the Desktop it asks which browser to open in; with shortcuts already there it asks nothing and rewrites the ones you have, along with the Startup entry, because a .lnk holds the full path to the app folder and an install that moved leaves every one of them aimed at where the folder used to be. That is what was behind an error page at sign-in on one machine: a Startup entry made from a copy unzipped into Downloads, still opening a folder that had been deleted months before. The uninstaller now finds shortcuts like that too, and knows all four profile names. The browser profile is smaller. A stock Chrome profile collects some thirty folders of things fetched in the background -- safe browsing lists, hyphenation dictionaries, captcha providers, on-device suggestion models -- and this is a browser showing one local file with no address bar. The launchers start it with those switched off, the installer removes the ones already there from a list written out by hand, and Local Storage, where the settings actually live, is not in that list and is never touched. The Chrome profile is also called profile-chrome now rather than profile, so the one folder of the three that did not say which browser it was for no longer exists; it is moved, not remade. The launch is quieter: the black console rectangle and the taskbar button that flashed at every launch are gone, because a .cmd is run by cmd.exe and cmd.exe gets a console whatever the shortcut says about minimising it. A four-line .vbs starts the same script with no window at all. A station found in the directory is now labelled with its format, its bitrate and the city you searched for -- AAC+ 48 kbps Toronto -- rather than a region or a country, neither of which tells two stations in the same province apart. Every box in Settings has a placeholder and a tooltip saying what it is for. Two smaller things: resetting no longer leaves the schedule chip claiming the opposite of what it had just been set to, and the default for what happens when the day's last slot ends was a dead letter -- an absent setting was read as "keep playing" on the way in, whatever the default said, so the deliberate choice of silence outside the hours somebody set never once took effect.
